title: 387. The Problem with Being a Team Player
author: The Best Leadership Newsletter Ever
source: The Best Leadership Newsletter Ever (thebestleadershipnewsletter.com), September 7, 2026
summary: This piece dismantles the popular leadership maxim 'it's amazing what we can accomplish when nobody wants credit' by walking through Max Ringelmann's 1913 tug-of-war experiment, which found that individual effort systematically decreases as group size grows -- a phenomenon replicated across decades of psychology research and now known as social loafing or the Ringelmann Effect. The author's key move is distinguishing between two things that sound identical to the part of the brain deciding how hard to pull: genuine humility about credit, versus mere confusion about who contributed what -- and arguing that both produce the same measurable outcome, less effort, because neither preserves the sense that individual contribution is being tracked. The resolution offered is that teams which appear to run on selfless effort without anyone chasing credit actually have a leader quietly watching and privately attributing contribution the entire time; the team members aren't trying hard because credit doesn't matter to them, but because they trust that someone who matters is paying attention. The piece closes by reframing 'credit doesn't matter' as a dangerous half-truth for managers: what matters isn't eliminating credit, but never letting attention to who-did-what lapse, since a leader who genuinely doesn't track contribution gets a team of disengaged loafers, not a team of selfless collaborators.
points: Ringelmann's tug-of-war finding -- that even blindfolded subjects who merely believed they were in a group (while actually pulling alone) exerted less effort -- shows the effect is driven by belief about visibility, not actual social presence, which is the load-bearing evidence for the whole argument.

The essay's sharpest distinction is that 'nobody wants credit' and 'nobody is paying attention to who deserves credit' produce identical brain signals (and identical reduced effort), even though leaders often conflate the former (a virtue to encourage) with the latter (a failure to avoid).

The proposed fix relocates the leader's job: rather than eliminating credit-talk to promote humility, the leader's actual responsibility is to privately and continuously track exactly who contributed what, even while publicly downplaying credit as unimportant.

The sports analogy of the ball-hog teammate who won't pass functions as the alternative failure mode: remove attention to individual contribution entirely and you don't get selfless collaboration, you get people either loafing or hoarding the ball to guarantee visible credit for themselves.
quotes: He discovered that, as the group got bigger, each person pulled with less effort.

They even tried to be sneaky with it. They blindfolded people and told them they were acting in a group, when they were actually alone the whole time. But their effort was still less than if they knew they were doing it solo.

The other is just confusion, where everyone's effort is so tangled together that nobody can actually tell who did what. Unfortunately, to the part of the brain deciding how hard to pull on the rope, both explanations sound the same. And Ringelmann already told us what that produces. Less rope. When nobody gets singled out, people won't try as hard.

If you study every example of a team where something extraordinary happened without anybody looking for credit, they all have one thing in common: Somebody was still watching. And counting. And giving credit where it was deserved.
In other words, "nobody wants credit" is not nearly the same as "nobody is paying attention to who should get credit." That distinction is critical.

Think about the last time your team delivered something exceptional. Do you know specifically who did what? If you're not sure, neither do they. And that's exactly why it won't happen the same way twice.
